topic: Scheduled vs unscheduled banks: origin, criteria, why it matters, and the types of banks

book_understanding.teaching_order: Textbooks usually give the types first and the definitions after. Here the order is history, the law that created the split, what 'schedule' means, the criteria, why the status matters (benefits), a common misconception, and only then the types tree. 'Why it matters' comes before the long list, so the list lands on a reason.
book_understanding.breakdown_rule: Each piece answers the next natural learner question: where did it come from, what does the word mean, who decides, what difference does it make, is it a different rulebook, what kinds exist.

opening.what: Recalls from the banking-history video that the RBI Act was passed in 1934 and RBI set up in 1935, while a law-book drops onto a timeline.

moves.concept: RBI Act 1934 and the split of banks
moves.what: RBI Act 1934 passed by the British government; RBI established in 1935 on its basis.

moves.concept: RBI Act 1934 and the split of banks
moves.what: Besides setting up RBI, the Act split all Indian banks into scheduled and unscheduled.
For this, Schedule 2 was added to the Act.
Schedule means suchi yaani list; only banks named in this list are scheduled banks.

moves.concept: inclusion criteria and RBI's power to change them
moves.what: But the question is: on what criteria were names added?

moves.concept: inclusion criteria and RBI's power to change them
moves.what: Paid-up capital, reserves, liquidity and solvency levels.

moves.concept: inclusion criteria and RBI's power to change them
moves.what: The criteria are not fixed: they change with economic conditions, RBI has the power to change them, and RBI keeps updating the list.
Voices the learner's doubt: what difference does it make whether a bank is scheduled or not?
Scheduled banks can take low-cost funds from RBI (repo window, MSF, other facilities) for normal needs; unscheduled banks cannot and must go to the market.
In emergencies RBI may lend to unscheduled banks, but at a much higher rate.
Scheduled banks enjoy more credibility and reputation, so more customers prefer them.
Many people think unscheduled means unregulated; that is completely wrong, since every bank needs an RBI licence and must follow RBI's rules.
Chaliye, now the types of scheduled and unscheduled banks.
Each side has co-operative and commercial banks.
Scheduled commercial banks: public sector, private sector, foreign, regional rural, small finance and payments banks.
No public sector bank or regional rural bank can be unscheduled; what remains are private, foreign, small finance and payments banks.
No payments bank is unscheduled today, though some may be in future; local area banks are unscheduled.
One line: today we covered bank types and their categorisation; co-operative banks next.

examples.what: The repo rate window and the marginal standing facility named as the cheap RBI credit routes.
examples.carries: the main benefit of scheduled status

examples.what: Customers choosing scheduled banks because they trust them more.
Public sector banks and RRBs can never be unscheduled; no payments bank is unscheduled today.

closing.what: A one-line recap and a pointer to the next video (co-operative banks), spoken over a promo overlay.

narration.density: About 20 terms (Act, schedule, four criteria, repo, MSF, credibility, commercial, co-operative, six plus five bank types) in about 230 s, about 5 per minute. The first 170 s are well paced; the last 60 s are a rapid list.

talmel_summary: In the first half the picture shows steps: a law-book drops on 1934, the bank forks, a Loan note rides the RBI arrow, often a few seconds before the words. In the second half the picture becomes a list: 10 of 24 changes are tree labels typed exactly on the spoken name, which matches perfectly but adds nothing to the words. One note adds a fact (the 1949 Act) that the voice never says, and the spoken caveat about payments banks is not marked on the tree.

voice.notes: About 177 words per minute, the slowest of this batch; calm and conversational. Uses 'dekhiye' and direct questions to the viewer. Puts deliberate pauses of about 0.6 s between list items when naming bank types. Stresses 'bilkul galat' at the misconception. No numbers at all (the rate gap is 'kaafi zyada').

game_ideas.player_does: Plays RBI at the list desk: bank cards show paid-up capital, reserves, liquidity and solvency; the player decides which banks go into Schedule II under the current criteria. An 'economy event' card then changes the criteria.
game_ideas.process_happens: A cash crunch follows: listed banks draw cheap repo loans (green note riding the RBI arrow), unlisted ones must borrow from the market or pay a red higher emergency rate; customer stars drift toward listed banks.
game_ideas.win: The list matches the criteria after every change and no weak bank fails in the crunch.
game_ideas.lose: Listing a weak bank makes it fail in the crunch (why the criteria exist); leaving a strong bank off makes it pay a high rate and lose customers (why the status matters).
game_ideas.concept: Schedule II criteria and the benefits of scheduled status

game_ideas.player_does: Drags bank cards (a public sector bank, an RRB, a small finance bank, a payments bank, a local area bank, a foreign bank) into a tree: scheduled or unscheduled, then commercial or co-operative.
game_ideas.process_happens: Each correct drop grows a leaf on the tree the way the video does.
game_ideas.win: Every card placed in a branch where it is allowed.
game_ideas.lose: Dropping a public sector bank or RRB on the unscheduled side bounces it back with the rule; a payments bank on the unscheduled side is accepted but tagged 'none today'.

checks_learned: A spoken misconception needs a 'wrong idea, crossed out, right idea' beat on screen, not just a note.
Screen text must not add a fact the voice never mentions (here the Banking Regulation Act, 1949) unless the voice pauses to point at it.

A classification list of more than about 4 leaves should not be typed leaf by leaf for close to a minute; group it, give one example per leaf, and show what is missing on the other side (no public sector bank or RRB among unscheduled banks).
A spoken caveat about a leaf ('no payments bank is unscheduled today') must mark that leaf on the picture.
After each classification the script should answer 'what difference does it make?'; this video does it with an explicit learner question, and it should be a rule.

teaching_best.why: 'Schedule' is unpacked to the plain word suchi / list, which makes the whole term obvious.
Voices the learner's doubt (what difference does it make?) before giving three concrete benefits.
Names a common wrong belief (unscheduled = unregulated) and corrects it with the licence rule.

teaching_weak.why: About 50 s of bank-type names with no example bank and no reason for each type.
Criteria given as a list, with no example of a bank that meets or fails them.
'Much higher rate' has no numbers, and the rate gap is never shown on a scale.
